A billionaire businessman who became Lebanon's first post-civil-war prime minister and helped rebuild Beirut, his 2005 assassination shook the country — who was he?
Rafic Hariri: Prime Minister of Lebanon (1992–1998; 2000–2004)

Fought from 1964 to 1979 in what would become independent Zimbabwe, this conflict pitted Ian Smith's white minority government against guerrilla forces led by Robert Mugabe and Joshua Nkomo — what was it called?
Rhodesian Bush War: 1964–1979 conflict in Southern Africa.
He founded Electronic Data Systems and never carried a single state, yet his 1992 and 1996 runs were among the strongest third-party showings in U.S. history — which Texan businessman was it?
Ross Perot: American businessman and politician (1930–2019)

A tailor's son turned Navy Board official and MP, he is remembered far less for his politics than for the candid private diary he kept for nearly a decade — a prime window into the Stuart Restoration. Who was he?
Samuel Pepys: English writer and politician (1633–1703)

Once Adolf Hitler's personal chauffeur and bodyguard, this German officer rose to become the highest-ranking commissioned commander in the Waffen-SS despite having no formal staff training — who is he?
Sepp Dietrich: German Nazi politician and SS commander (1892–1966)

Lasting 872 days and killing an estimated 1.5 million from a prewar population of 3.2 million, this WWII blockade of the Soviet Union's second-largest city was never successfully captured — what was it?
Siege of Leningrad: Blockade by the Axis powers, 1941–1944.
Wounded at Gallipoli before entering politics, this businessman led the Nationalist Party as the eighth prime minister of Australia from 1923 to 1929 — who was he?
Stanley Bruce: Prime Minister of Australia from 1923 to 1929. In office, Bruce pursued an energetic and diverse agenda.

Ceded by the Qing dynasty after its defeat in an 1895 war with a rising East Asian empire, this island served as that empire's first colony, governed for the next 50 years from a capital called Taihoku — what period of history is this?
Taiwan under Japanese rule: 1895–1945 colony of the Empire of Japan.
He landed at Anzac Cove in 1915, distinguished himself planning the Battle of Pozières, and remains the only Australian ever to reach the rank of field marshal — who was he?

Serving as the eighth U.S. director of national intelligence starting in 2025, this former Hawaii congresswoman deployed to Iraq with the National Guard and later left the Democrats to become a Republican — who is she?
Tulsi Gabbard: American politician and military officer (born 1981)

Set to become just the fourth queen to rule her Scandinavian kingdom in her own right — and the first since 1720 — she is heir apparent thanks to a 1980 law that was Western Europe's first with absolute primogeniture. Who is she?
Victoria, Crown Princess of Sweden: Heir apparent to the Swedish throne (born 1977)

In June 2014, forces captured the cities of Mosul and Tikrit, prompting Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki to call for a national state of emergency that parliament refused to grant — which conflict was this?
War in Iraq (2013–2017): Armed Conflict in the Middle East.
A social worker shaped by the 1960s and the Occupation of Alcatraz, she became the first woman elected Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation — who is she?
Wilma Mankiller: Cherokee Nation chief and activist (1945–2010)
Once called 'perhaps the most famous singer alive' in much of Africa, this Senegalese star helped develop the mbalax genre and even served as his country's Minister of Tourism — who is he?
Youssou N'Dour: Senegalese politician and musician (born 1959)
Which of these four is the eldest?
Levi Strauss (born 1829) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four. Benjamin Banneker (November 9, 1731 – October 19, 1806) was an American naturalist, mathematician, astronomer and almanac author.
Which of these four was founded earliest?
C (programming language) (founded 1972) is the earliest of the four. C is a general-purpose programming language created in the 1970s by Dennis Ritchie.
Which of these four was founded earliest?

Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four. Originally specified in the late 1950s, it is the second-oldest high-level programming language still in common use, after Fortran.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Roger Joseph Boscovich is a physicist.
Which of these four is a chemist?
Percy Lavon Julian is a chemist. Percy Lavon Julian (April 11, 1899 – April 19, 1975) was an American research chemist and a pioneer in the chemical synthesis of medicinal drugs from plants.
What is the atomic number of Mendelevium?
Mendelevium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Md (formerly Mv) and atomic number 101.
In what year was Grigori Perelman born?
Grigori Perelman: The full details of Perelman's work were filled in and explained by various authors over the following several years.
In what year was Sean Parker born?
Sean Parker: According to Forbes, as of May 2025, Parker's estimated net worth stood at US$3.0 billion, placing him in the top 1,250 richest individuals in the world.
In what year was C. V. Raman born?
C. V. Raman: This phenomenon, a hitherto unknown type of scattering of light they called modified scattering, was subsequently termed the Raman effect or Raman scattering.
In what year did Hypatia die?
Hypatia: Not the only fourth century Alexandrian female mathematician, Hypatia was preceded by Pandrosion.
In what year did Jan Hus die?
Jan Hus: Hus is considered to be the first Church reformer, even though some designate the theorist John Wycliffe.
In what year was Radium discovered?
Radium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ra and atomic number 88.
In what year was Copper discovered?
Copper is a chemical element; it has symbol Cu (from Latin cuprum) and atomic number 29.
Mil Mi-17: Kazan Helicopters. It is known as the Mi-8M series in Russian service.
Which country is Curtiss P-40 Warhawk from?
Curtiss P-40 Warhawk: United States. The Curtiss P-40 Warhawk is an American single-engined, single-seat, all-metal fighter-bomber that first flew in 1938.
Who is credited with discovering Ruthenium?
Ruthenium: Karl Ernst Claus. Ruthenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ru and atomic number 44.
Who is credited with discovering Aniline?
Aniline: Otto Unverdorben. Aniline (From Portuguese: anil, meaning 'indigo shrub', and -ine indicating a derived substance) is an organic compound with the formula C6H5NH2.
Who is credited with discovering Lie group?
Lie group: Sophus Lie. Combining these two ideas, one obtains a continuous group where multiplying points and their inverses is continuous.
With the formula (CH3)2CO, this volatile solvent is produced by the millions of tonnes yearly, much of it to make precursors for plastics like bisphenol A — what is it?
Acetone (2-propanone or dimethyl ketone) is an organic compound with the formula (CH3)2CO.
A close relative of the peach in the genus Prunus, this drupe's seed isn't a true nut and can be "blanched" by softening its skin in hot water before peeling — what is it?
These eusocial insects evolved from vespoid wasps back in the Cretaceous, and you can spot one by its elbowed antennae and pinched, node-like waist. Which creature is it?
Ant are eusocial insects of the family Formicidae and, along with the related wasps and bees, belong to the order Hymenoptera.
This genus of roughly 300 evergreen flowering plants includes one edible species enjoyed as a vegetable and another grown purely as an ornamental — which genus?
Asparagus (genus) is a genus of flowering plants in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Asparagoideae.
This self-taught Maryland-born mathematician published a successful series of almanacs and assisted Major Andrew Ellicott in surveying the new federal capital district — who was he?
Benjamin Banneker (November 9, 1731 - October 19, 1806) was an American naturalist, mathematician, astronomer and almanac author.
Belonging to the Colubridae family of venomous snakes and found only in Sub-Saharan Africa, this reptile's scientific name is Dispholidus typus — what is it commonly called?
Boomslang (or; Dispholidus typus) is a highly venomous snake in the family Colubridae.
This American actress is remembered chiefly as the mother of a famous Hollywood actress and actor, and the former wife of actor Jon Voight. Who is she?
Caesium (IUPAC spelling; also spelled cesium in American English) is a chemical element; it has symbol Cs and atomic number 55.
Named for the whisker-like barbels many species sport, these scaleless ray-finned fish include some of the largest freshwater giants in Southeast Asia and Eurasia — name this diverse group of fish?
Catfish are a diverse group of ray-finned fish of the order Siluriformes (historically Nematognathi).
This insect family, known as the 'true' members of its group, contains roughly 3,400 species worldwide, distinct from just two species in a smaller sister family. What family is it?

Cicadidae is one of two families of cicadas, with about 3,400 species in over 520 genera worldwide; it contains most living cicada species, except for the two belonging to its sister taxon, the Tettigarctidae.

Serving as personal doctor to a superstar singer on the day of his 2009 death, this physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter over the misuse of a surgical anesthetic as a sleep aid — who is he?
Conrad Murray (born February 19, 1953) is a Grenadian-born American former physician convicted for his role in the death of American singer and dancer Michael Jackson.
Unrelated to poor hygiene, this scalp condition causes flaking and mild itching and is often treated with antifungal or keratolytic remedies; about half of all adults experience it. What is it?
Dandruff is a skin condition of the scalp. It can result in social or self-esteem problems.
Made from a fermented batter of ground black gram and rice, this thin South Indian bread is traditionally served with chutney and sambar — what is it?

Dosa (food) (in Indian English) or thosai (in Malaysian English and Singapore English) is a thin, savoury batter bread in South Indian cuisine made from a fermented batter of ground black gram and rice.
Born to a mathematician father in Erlangen, this pioneering algebraist proved theorems connecting symmetry to conservation laws in physics — who is she?
Emmy Noether (23 March 1882 - 14 April 1935) was a German mathematician who made many important contributions to abstract algebra.
First confirmed around a pulsar in 1992, this astronomical term describes any planet located outside our own solar system — over 6,300 have now been confirmed — what is it called?
Exoplanet is a planet outside the Solar System. The first confirmed detection of an exoplanet was in 1992 around a pulsar, and the first detection around a main-sequence star was in 1995.
This American political scientist argued in a controversial 1992 book that the spread of liberal democracy and free markets might be the final form of human government — who is he?
Francis Fukuyama (born October 27, 1952) is an American political scientist, political economist, and international relations scholar.
Often called the 'silent thief of sight' because it creeps up slowly, this group of eye diseases damages the optic nerve and is closely tied to raised pressure inside the eye — what is it?
Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that can lead to damage of the optic nerve, which transmits visual information from the eye to the brain.

This British businessman and adventurer, chairman of a Dubai-based aircraft brokerage, visited the South Pole multiple times and descended to the Mariana Trench's Challenger Deep before dying in 2023 when a submersible imploded in the North Atlantic - name him?
Hamish Harding (24 June 1964 - 18 June 2023) was a British businessman, pilot and adventurer based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
Domesticated in Central Asia around 4000 BCE, this one-toed hoofed mammal evolved over 45 million years from the small, multi-toed Eohippus — what is it?
Horse (Equus ferus caballus) is a domesticated, one-toed, hoofed mammal.

Co-creator of the breakthrough neural network AlexNet and a contributor to landmark AI systems including GPT and AlphaGo, this computer scientist has won a major deep-learning research award three years running — who is he?
Ilya Sutskever (born 1986) is a computer scientist who specializes in machine learning.

Designed under the philosophy 'write once, run anywhere,' this high-level, memory-safe, object-oriented programming language compiles to bytecode executed by a dedicated virtual machine — name the language?
Java (programming language) is a high-level, general-purpose, memory-safe, object-oriented programming language.
Diagnosed via corneal topography and linked to frequent eye rubbing and allergies, this progressive disorder causes the cornea to bulge into a cone shape — which eye condition?
Keratoconus is an eye disorder in which the cornea, the transparent front part of the eye, gradually thins and bulges outward into a cone shape.
This Swiss polymath founded the study of graph theory and topology, and introduced much of modern mathematical notation, including the concept of a function — who is he?
Leonhard Euler (15 April 1707 - 18 September 1783) was a Swiss polymath who was active as a mathematician, physicist, astronomer, logician, geographer, music theorist and engineer.
Native to Afghanistan and Iran but long grown in Europe, this herb's leaves, roots, and seeds are all used in cooking, tasting like a more intense mix of celery and parsley — what is it?
Lovage (Levisticum officinale) is a perennial plant, the sole species in the genus Levisticum in the family Apiaceae, subfamily Apioideae.
Google's employee No. 20 and its first woman software engineer, she later left to run a famous internet company as CEO from 2012 until Verizon bought it — who is she?
Marissa Mayer (born May 30, 1975) is an American business executive, software engineer, and investor who served as president and chief executive officer of Yahoo!

Named from Greek words meaning 'small head,' this congenital condition involves a smaller-than-normal head and can affect brain development, intellectual ability, and motor function — which disorder is it?
Microcephaly (from Neo-Latin microcephalia, from Ancient Greek mikrs "small" and kephal "head") is a medical condition involving a smaller-than-normal head.
This group of more than 30 rare neuromuscular disorders causes skeletal tissue to progressively weaken and break down, differing in which body parts are hit first and how fast — what's it called?
Muscular dystrophy (MD) is a genetically and clinically heterogeneous group of rare neuromuscular diseases that cause progressive weakness and breakdown of skeletal muscles over time.
Once confused with its chemical twin tantalum, this element with atomic number 41 resists corrosion so well it's used in earrings for people allergic to nickel — which element?
Niobium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nb (formerly columbium, Cb) and atomic number 41.
Named from the Greek word for 'smell,' this hard, brittle, bluish-white transition metal has the highest density of any stable element and is often alloyed for fountain pen nib tips — which element?
Osmium (from Ancient Greek (osm) 'smell') is a chemical element; it has symbol Os and atomic number 76.
Made by grinding dry-roasted legumes and often tweaked with salt or emulsifiers, this protein-rich spread is the most popular of all the nut butters — what is it?
Peanut butter is a food paste or spread made from ground, dry-roasted peanuts.

Enclosed in a papery husk formed from its calyx, the fruit of this nightshade-family genus tastes like a firm tomato crossed with a sweet, tangy grape — nearly half of its species grow only in Mexico. Name the genus?
Physalis (from Ancient) is a genus of approximately 75 to 90 flowering plants in the nightshade family (Solanaceae), which are native to the Americas and Australasia.
This autonomic nervous system disorder causes an abnormally large jump in heart rate — thirty beats per minute within ten minutes — simply from sitting up or standing. What condition is it?
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is a condition characterized by an abnormally large increase in heart rate upon sitting up or standing.
Easily identified by its striking red and black coloring, this common European insect is often mistaken for an unrelated lookalike called the cinnamon bug — what insect is it?
Pyrrhocoris apterus is a common insect of the family Pyrrhocoridae.
Made up of a large and small subunit built from RNA and proteins, this molecular machine found in every living cell translates messenger RNA into chains of amino acids — what is it?
Ribosome is a ribonucleoprotein particle found in all cells, both prokaryotic and eukaryotic, responsible for the synthesis of proteins.

This volatile, colorless, and odorless nerve agent is so potent a chemical weapon that inhaling a lethal dose can cause death from respiratory paralysis within one to ten minutes — what's the compound called?
Sarin (NATO designation GB short for G-series, B) is an extremely toxic organophosphorus compound that has been often used as a chemical weapon due to its extreme potency as a nerve agent.

Defined by the American Thoracic Society as a subjective, uncomfortable experience of breathing discomfort that can include chest tightness or a sense of effort to breathe — what is this sensation called?
Shortness of breath (SOB), known as dyspnea (in AmE) or dyspnoea (in BrE), is an uncomfortable feeling of not being able to breathe well enough.
First described in 1780, this slender, long-legged antelope of southern Africa wears a white face crossed by a dark stripe from eye to mouth — and both sexes sport backward-curving horns. What is it?
Springbok (Antidorcas marsupialis) is an antelope found mainly in south and southwest Africa.

This amniote lineage — one of just two major branches alongside the reptile-and-bird clade — is marked by a single temporal opening behind the eye and gave rise to every mammal alive today — name the group?
Synapsida is a diverse group of tetrapod vertebrates that includes all mammals and their extinct relatives.
Writing in 1798, this English cleric-economist warned that abundance only fuels population growth, eventually restoring poverty and hardship for the lower classes — who is he?
Thomas Robert Malthus (13/14 February 1766 - 29 December 1834) was an English economist, cleric, and scholar influential in the fields of political economy and demography.
Built in the Soviet Union from 1966 to 1989 for short-haul routes, this narrow-body jet earned the NATO codename 'Crusty' — which airliner is it?
Tupolev Tu-134 (NATO reporting name: Crusty) is a twin-engined, narrow-body jet airliner built in the Soviet Union for short and medium-haul routes from 1966 to 1989.
Named from a French verb meaning 'to see,' this term describes the practice of secretly watching others in intimate moments, often labeled 'Peeping Tom' behavior — what is it?
Voyeurism is the habit of clandestine watching other people engaged in intimate behaviors, such as undressing, sexual activity, or other actions of a private nature, commonly for sexual stimulation.

Native to freshwater and brackish habitats across western Eurasia, this ray-finned fish in the perch family, related to perch, ruffe, and darters, has become a popular game species well beyond its original range. Name it?
Zander (Sander lucioperca), sander or pikeperch, is a species of ray-finned fish from the family Percidae (which also includes perch, ruffe and darter).
Marked by inadequate cortisol and aldosterone production in the adrenal glands, this rare, long-term endocrine disorder is also known as primary adrenal insufficiency — what is it?
Addison's disease: Endocrine disorder. Addison's disease arises when the adrenal gland does not produce sufficient amounts of the steroid hormones cortisol and (sometimes) aldosterone.
His mother and wife were both deaf, which steered this Scottish-born inventor toward hearing devices — and, in 1876, the first U.S. patent for the telephone. Who was he?
Alexander Graham Bell: Inventor of the telephone (1847–1922)
This inorganic salt, most commonly used as a soil fertilizer, is 21% nitrogen and 24% sulfur by content — what is it?

Native to the Americas from northern Mexico to northern Argentina, this flowering plant genus is the largest in the arum family and includes types nicknamed flamingo flower and pigtail plant. What genus is it?
Anthurium: Genus of plants. Anthurium (Schott, 1829) is a genus of about 1,000 species of flowering plants, the largest genus of the arum family, Araceae.
Unlike its counterpart which returns blood to the heart, this blood vessel usually carries oxygen-rich blood away from it — what is it?
Artery: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart.
Best known for pioneering radical behaviorism at Harvard, this psychologist invented a chamber for studying operant conditioning that came to bear his name — who is he?
B. F. Skinner: American psychologist and social philosopher (1904–1990)
Built atop an Ilyushin transport and nicknamed 'Mainstay,' this Soviet radar plane had its existence leaked to the West by a spy in 1978 — which aircraft is it?
Beriev A-50: Soviet airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft.
This North American wild cat earns its name from the black-tipped, stubby tail it sports, along with distinctive black bars on its forelegs — one of the four species of lynx. Which animal is it?
Bobcat: Medium-sized North American wild cat.

After resigning from Evergreen State College following 2017 protests over campus racial equity, this podcaster and former evolutionary biology professor was named part of the 'intellectual dark web' — who is he?
Bret Weinstein: American podcaster and author (born 1969)
This highly soluble white crystalline salt is spread on icy roads for de-icing and, in its anhydrous form, works as a moisture-absorbing desiccant. What compound is it?
Calcium chloride: Chemical compound. The compound is a white crystalline solid at room temperature, and it is highly soluble in water.
Native to the Mediterranean, this legume tree's seed pods are ground into a chocolate substitute, while its seeds yield a common food thickener known as locust bean gum — which tree?
Carob: Small tree grown for its edible pods and landscaping.
This goat-antelope roams mountain ranges from the Pyrenees to the Caucasus and has even been introduced to New Zealand's South Island — which animal?
Named after a 17th-century English physician, this ring-shaped network of arteries supplies blood to the brain in humans and other vertebrates — what is it called?
Circle of Willis: Circulatory anastomosis that supplies blood to the brain and surrounding structures.
Also known as foremilk or historically as 'beestings,' this early substance produced by mammary glands right after birth delivers antibodies and immune factors to newborns. What is it?
Colostrum: Form of milk produced immediately following the delivery of newborn.
Latin for 'raven,' this widely distributed bird genus includes crows and rooks and gave a group of its members the eerie collective noun 'a murder' — what genus is it?
Corvus: Genus of birds including crows, ravens and rooks.

First synthesized in 1874, this insecticide earned its discoverer a 1948 Nobel Prize and was used in WWII against malaria and typhus before becoming infamous for its environmental damage — what is it?
DDT: Organochloride known as an insecticide.

This group of microalgae generates roughly a fifth to a half of Earth's oxygen each year, and its dead shells drift on Saharan winds to fertilize the entire Amazon basin with millions of tons of dust annually. What are they?
Diatom: Single-celled alga with a silica cell wall.
Smaller and shorter-necked than their swan and goose cousins in the family Anatidae, these aquatic birds are often confused with grebes, loons, and coots — what are they?
Duck: Common name for many species of bird.
The second-largest member of the deer family, this animal is also called "wapiti," a Shawnee and Cree word meaning "white rump" for the pale fur it flashes to signal alarm — what animal is it?
Elk: Species of deer. The word "elk" originally referred to the European variety of the moose, Alces alces, but was transferred to Cervus canadensis by North American colonists.

In 2019 this French-American MIT economist shared the Nobel with her husband and Michael Kremer for an experimental approach to fighting global poverty, rooted in the randomized trials of her J-PAL lab — who is she?
First confirmedly detected in 1992 orbiting a pulsar, this term describes any planet found outside our solar system — what is it?
Exoplanet: Planet outside of the Solar System. The first confirmed detection of an exoplanet was in 1992 around a pulsar, and the first detection around a main-sequence star was in 1995.
From the Latin word for 'tube' or 'pipe,' this medical term describes an abnormal connection between two hollow spaces in the body — what is it?
Fistula: Abnormal connection between two hollow bodily spaces, often organs.
This mathematical principle links differentiation and integration, showing the two operations to be essentially inverses of each other — what is it called?
Fundamental theorem of calculus: Relationship between derivatives and integrals.
Recognized as the world's longest ray-finned fish, this ribbon-shaped, silvery-blue deep-sea creature is often blamed for sea-serpent legends — which fish?
Giant oarfish: Species of oceanic ray-finned fish.
Descended from medieval hunting dogs once used to take down bears, boar, and deer for German nobility, this breed ties with the Irish Wolfhound as one of the world's two largest — which breed is it?
Great Dane: German breed of dog. The Great Dane is a German breed of large mastiff-sighthound, which descends from hunting dogs of the Middle Ages used to hunt bears, wild boar, and deer.
This German-American physicist won a 1967 Nobel Prize for explaining how a nuclear cycle powers heavy stars, after heading the Theoretical Division at Los Alamos during World War II — who is he?
In this condition, part of the stomach slips upward through the diaphragm into the chest, often triggering acid reflux, heartburn, or trouble swallowing — what is it?
Hiatal hernia: Entrance of abdominal organs into the middle chest through the diaphragm.
Also called prussic acid, this toxic, flammable liquid with the formula HCN boils just above room temperature and serves as an industrial precursor to plastics and mining chemicals — what is it?

Also known as the spectacled or binocellate snake, this reptile from South Asia is one of the 'Big Four' species responsible for most snakebites in the region and is revered in Hindu mythology — which snake?
Indian cobra: Species of snake. The species is native to the Indian subcontinent, and is a member of the "Big Four" species that are responsible for the most snakebite cases in Sri Lanka and India.
This English inventor and industrial designer created the bagless vacuum cleaner using cyclonic separation, and by 2023 was the UK's fifth-richest person — who is he?
James Dyson: British inventor and businessman (born 1947)
Back in 1859, this Irish physicist proved the link between atmospheric CO2 and what we now call the greenhouse effect — who was he?
Deafened by childhood illness and rerouted from competitive diving, she became a Hollywood stunt pioneer and earned the title 'the fastest woman in the world.' Who was she?
Kitty O'Neil: American stuntwoman and racer (1946–2018)

Caused by a bacterium that thrives in fresh water and can contaminate hot tubs and water tanks, this atypical pneumonia brings cough, high fever and muscle pains days after exposure — what's it called?
Legionnaires' disease: Form of atypical pneumonia. Legionnaires' disease is a form of atypical pneumonia caused by any species of Legionella bacteria, quite often Legionella pneumophila.
Named after both a biblical sea monster and the author of 'Moby-Dick,' this extinct predatory sperm whale roamed ancient oceans roughly 9 million years ago — which genus?
Livyatan: Extinct genus of sperm whale from the Miocene epoch.
Native to northeastern Australia and first commercially grown at scale in Hawaii during the 1880s, this is the only widely cultivated food plant indigenous to Australia — what nut is it?
Macadamia: Genus of plants indigenous to Australia.
The heaviest members of the squirrel family, these ground-dwelling herbivores live in groups through the summer before disappearing underground to hibernate all winter — what are they?
Marmot: Genus of mammals (large ground squirrels)
This WWII German monoplane fighter formed the backbone of the Luftwaffe alongside the Focke-Wulf Fw 190, though Allied aircrew nicknamed it after its designer — which aircraft?

Messerschmitt Bf 109: German WWII fighter aircraft family. The Messerschmitt Bf 109 is a monoplane fighter aircraft that was designed and initially produced by the German aircraft manufacturer Bayerische Flugzeugwerke (BFW).
Produced by mammary glands and rich in calcium, protein and lactose, this liquid is often prized for its antibody-packed early form, colostrum — what is it?
Milk: Nutrient-rich liquid produced by mammals.
Grown above the upper lip and below the nose, this facial hair style has taken many forms across history — what is it called?
Moustache: Strip of facial hair across the upper lip. A moustache (UK:) or mustache (US:) is a growth of facial hair grown above the upper lip and under the nose of men.

Attributed to 19th-century pathologist Rudolf Virchow, this term for the premature death of cells caused by trauma or infection contrasts with the body's own programmed cell death — what's the condition called?
Necrosis: Unprogrammed cell death caused by external cell injury.
Designed in the late 1950s as a six-engine, delta-winged prototype bomber capable of Mach 3+ at 70,000 feet, this aircraft was meant to outrun any interceptor of its era — which plane?
North American XB-70 Valkyrie: Prototype supersonic strategic bomber.
Mostly black on top, white below, and sporting unmistakable white eye patches, this cosmopolitan apex predator is actually the largest member of the oceanic dolphin family. What is it?
Orca: Largest living species of dolphin.

Named for its resemblance to a related crested dinosaur, this duck-billed herbivore could grow over 9 meters long, moved on two or four legs, and was first described in 1922 by William Parks — which dinosaur genus?
Parasaurolophus: Hadrosaurid ornithopod dinosaur genus from Late Cretaceous Period.
This order of hoofed mammals — horses, rhinos, and tapirs — bears its weight on an odd number of toes and digests plant fiber in its intestines rather than a multi-chambered stomach. Which order?
Perissodactyla: Order of hoofed mammals. Perissodactyla (from Ancient Greek περισσός, perissós 'odd' and δάκτυλος, dáktylos 'finger, toe'), or odd-toed ungulates, is an order of ungulates.
As the only surviving son of a legendary Italian carmaker, this billionaire owns just over 10% of the company that bears his father's name and serves as its vice chairman — who is he?
Piero Ferrari: Italian billionaire businessman. Piero Ferrari (born Piero Lardi, 22 May 1945; later Piero Lardi Ferrari) is an Italian billionaire businessman and sport personality.
Born Joseph Ratzinger, this head of the Catholic Church made history in 2013 by resigning the role, then adopted the title 'emeritus' until his death — who was he?
Pope Benedict XVI: Head of the Catholic Church from 2005 to 2013.

With 348 known species spanning an opportunistic human pathogen, a plant disease-causer, and a soil-dwelling growth-promoter, which gram-negative bacterial genus in Gammaproteobacteria is renowned for its metabolic diversity?
Pseudomonas: Genus of Gram-negative bacteria. Pseudomonas is a genus of gram-negative bacteria belonging to the family Pseudomonadaceae in the class Gammaproteobacteria.
This Norwegian shared the very first Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics, and we owe him the words 'econometrics,' 'microeconomics,' and 'macroeconomics' — who was he?
Ragnar Frisch: Norwegian economist and Nobel Laureate (1895–1973)
This plant genus includes redcurrants, blackcurrants, and gooseberries, and also serves as the main alternate host for a fungal disease that attacks five-needle pines — which genus?
Ribes: Genus of flowering plants in the order Saxifragales.

Also called cot or crib death, this leading cause of infant mortality in the West strikes a baby under one, usually while sleeping between midnight and 9 a.m., and stays unexplained even after a full autopsy. What is it?
SIDS: Sudden unexplained death of a child who is less than one year of age.
A month or so of a diet starved of vitamin C brings on this old deficiency disease — fatigue, sore limbs, and bleeding gums among its hallmarks. What is its scorbutic name?
Scurvy: Disease resulting from a lack of vitamin C.

Adapted from the Army's Black Hawk with folding rotor blades and a hinged tail to fit aboard ships, this twin-engine Navy helicopter handles everything from anti-submarine warfare to medical evacuation — which aircraft?
